steps.content: The idea is about average trade size, which is quote volume per trade — USDT traded per coin, so it's already in a unit-free form comparable across coins. A "sudden jump" implies a short-window increase relative to the coin's own normal, so I'll start with that simplest form: log average trade size over 3 days minus its log over 20 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0259
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0095 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0146, 2023 -0.0116, 2024 -0.0048

The simple relative-to-own-history form has a negative incremental IC (−0.0095) and every sub-period is negative — so on this history a jump in average trade size has not predicted underperformance. Before concluding, I'll check whether the plain level of average trade size points the opposite way, since the reversal/liquidity styles already strip out short-term drift.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0238
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0004 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0089, 2023 -0.0035, 2024 +0.0070

At the level the incremental IC is essentially zero (−0.0004), which is where known styles live; the level form doesn't carry the effect the idea claims. One more reading of "sudden": the size measured only during the recent session, so I'll take the log average trade size over the last 2 days minus its log over 20 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0259
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0095 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0146, 2023 -0.0116, 2024 -0.0048

The session-based version is identical to the 3-day relative form (−0.0095), so the window length doesn't rescue it. That's two tests in a row failing to improve on the best result by 0.002, so I'll stop testing and hand in the simplest form that still points the way the idea says.

What I found: measured at the level, average trade size is essentially a liquidity proxy — its incremental IC is −0.0004, i.e. nothing left after the known styles are removed. Measured as a short-window increase over the coin's own norm, it is also negative (−0.0095), and negative in all three sub-periods, so on 2022-07 to 2024-12 a jump in average trade size has preceded *worse* returns, not better. I keep the direction the idea specifies rather than flipping it to chase the sign, and I submit the plain level form, which is the most faithful reading of "average trade size" and has the highest incremental IC (closest to zero, still negative).

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('num_trades'))</factor>
The idea is about yesterday's own move: coins that fell hard yesterday should bounce. The plainest reading is the negative of yesterday's return, so that's what I test first.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw IC is +0.0175 in the direction of the idea, but the incremental IC is 0.0000 — the whole signal is the known short-term reversal style, which gets removed. So I need yesterday's move measured in a way that isn't just the raw return: I'll measure yesterday's move as a position within the day's own range (close above the low, below the high), which still captures a big overnight dip but drops the overlap with the plain return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0379
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0127 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0166, 2023 -0.0113, 2024 -0.0122

That form has a clearly negative incremental IC (−0.0127), so the plain return is the right carrier of the signal, and reshaping it to sit closer to the low only adds noise. Since the plain return is largely the reversal style, I'll measure yesterday's fall as a *relative* size: the worst single-day print of the past week, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0140
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0081 (t = -3.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0122, 2023 -0.0100, 2024 -0.0041

Two forms in a row now fail the incremental test, so I stop testing and take the best tested one. What I found: the direction is right — yesterday's deep falls do precede bounces, with a plain rank IC of +0.0175. But that entire signal is the short-term reversal style, so once it's removed the incremental IC is 0.0000, which means almost nothing is left of the idea after the known styles. Measuring yesterday's fall as a position inside the day's range or as the worst print of the past week both carried the opposite sign after style removal, which tells me those refinements are adding noise or changing the signal.

So I hand in the plain form, pointing the way the idea says: the bigger the fall yesterday, the higher the factor value, the more bullish. It is the simplest faithful expression of the idea, and it is the one with the highest incremental IC among tested candidates.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea talks about the daily high-low range, which is `high - low` divided by `close` so the value is unit-free and comparable across coins. Wide range should mean bearish, so the whole factor gets a leading `-1`. I'll start with the simplest form: log range averaged over 5 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

Baseline: incremental IC +0.0203 with t = 8.7 and all three periods positive, so the direction holds. Now I'll check whether the plain average is driven by a few wide days, so I'll use the 5-day median of the log range instead.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0552
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0175 (t = 7.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0264, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0169

Median is worse (+0.0175 vs +0.0203), so the effect is not coming from a few extreme days; I'll go back to the average. Next I'll measure the range as log(high/low) minus log(close) — the part of the day's range that isn't just the price move — over a 5-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

That third form is identical to the first (+0.0203) — the log range minus log close is just log(close) canceled out, so it re-expresses the same quantity. Since the plain average and the median both failed to improve on it, I'll stop testing and hand in the simplest, most direct version.

What I found: wide daily ranges do precede underperformance on this history. The leading −1 makes the factor point the way the idea says, and the plain 5-day average of log(high/low) earns rank IC +0.0614 and incremental IC +0.0203 (t = 8.7), with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Using a median instead of a mean (+0.0175) or subtracting log(close) (+0.0203 again) both lost, so the plain average is the best of the tested forms and is what I submit.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

Idea: coins that fell a lot yesterday should bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is low. The simplest reading is just minus yesterday's return — a plain one-day return, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain version has a strong raw IC (+0.0175) but its incremental IC is 0.000 — the whole signal is the short-term reversal style, which is already removed. To isolate the bounce that comes from a *fall*, I will measure the size of yesterday's fall rather than the raw return: the distance down from the previous close, clamped at zero so coins that just drifted down count as fallen.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 907 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0051 (t = -3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0049, 2023 -0.0060, 2024 -0.0042

Clipping at zero made it worse (−0.0051), so the plain return is the right shape and I should keep the simple form while adjusting where the signal lives: since a one-day bounce is nearly all reversal, I will add yesterday's own relative strength — yesterday's return divided by its own 5-day average — so the factor leans on coins that fell hard *relative to their own norm*.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0024
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0002 (t = -0.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 -0.0025, 2024 -0.0007

Normalizing by the coin's own norm destroyed the signal (−0.0002), so the plain return is what carries it and I should stop adding complexity rather than burn another test on that shape. One thing still worth checking: the raw IC is high but the known styles already explain almost nothing, so the honest reading is that this idea has little incremental content on this history. The plainest reading, which is also the most faithful to the idea, is what I submit.

What I found: the plain minus-yesterday-return factor does rank with +0.0175 IC, but its incremental IC is 0.000 (t = 1.2) after removing reversal, volatility and liquidity — i.e., the bounce is entirely the short-term reversal effect, which is already priced out. Measuring only the size of a fall (clamped at zero) and measuring the fall relative to the coin's own norm both failed to add anything beyond the removed styles, so I keep the simplest form with the direction the idea specifies: a coin that fell yesterday scores high.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

Idea: the close sitting near the day's high means buyers controlled the price, so the factor should rise with that proximity. The plainest reading is the position of the close inside the day's range, `(close - low)/high`, which is unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll test that first.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0366
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0120 (t = -5.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0153, 2023 -0.0107, 2024 -0.0115

The plain position in the range has a negative absolute IC and a negative incremental IC in every sub-period — so on this history coins closing above their low underperformed, the opposite of the idea. Before concluding, I'll check one faithful variant: measuring the same thing (close near the high) over a week against the coin's own norm, which strips the coin's persistent volatility level from the comparison.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0008 (t = -0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0055, 2023 -0.0033, 2024 -0.0015

Subtracting the coin's own 5-day norm made the incremental IC nearly zero (−0.0008) but it also lost its sign in 2023, so it isn't fixing the problem. One more faithful reading of "closing near the high": where the close sits within the day's range, but using the log range so a few extreme-range days don't dominate the average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0032
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0030 (t = 1.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0058, 2023 +0.0032, 2024 +0.0014

The log-range version has the highest incremental IC of the three at +0.0030 (t = 1.3) and now all three sub-periods point the same way (+0.0058, +0.0032, +0.0014). Since the plain position in the range was clearly the worst of the three, I'll stop here rather than spend another test on window or smoothing tweaks.

What I found: the plain level of close-to-high position has a negative absolute IC (−0.0366) — coins closing near their high went on to underperform, so the idea as stated doesn't hold at the level. After removing the known styles, only the log-range form keeps a non-negative incremental IC (+0.0030), and that is small and its t-stat is far from strong (1.3), and 2023 still flips sign. So the honest answer is that this idea does not hold on this history in its plain form, and the least-bad faithful form is the log-range one, which I hand in with its direction pointing up (buying near the high).

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().safe_div(Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln())</factor>

Idea: closing near the day's high means buyers controlled the price, and that should be bullish. The most direct measure is where the close sits between the day's low and high, as a fraction — unitless, so coins are comparable.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0300
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0143 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0263, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0103

The plainest form already works: incremental IC +0.0143 with t = 5.7 and all three sub-periods positive. Next I'll check whether the plain fraction is just re-expressing volatility — so I'll measure the same "close above high" position but as a rank within the day, averaged over a few days, to see if the signal survives removing volatility.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0438
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0185 (t = 7.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0271, 2023 +0.0167, 2024 +0.0159

Ranking within the day before averaging lifted incremental IC to +0.0185 (t = 7.2) and raised every sub-period, so the signal is not just volatility. Since the day's high can be very wide on wide-range coins, I'll now measure the same control as a share of the day's own range — (close − low)/(high − low) — which treats a coin's range equally regardless of its price unit.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0033 (t = 1.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0059, 2023 +0.0035, 2024 +0.0018

The range-share form collapses to +0.0033 — it is essentially the same information as the range, which is already stripped out, so that shape is not the one. One thing still untested: the plain fraction is dominated by coins that close exactly at the high, so I'll widen the reference to the session's high plus a small buffer before averaging over a few days to see whether a wider "above the high" reading stays stronger.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0120
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0110 (t = 3.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0214, 2023 +0.0062, 2024 +0.0106

That buffer version falls to +0.0110 — the reference must be the actual high, not a smoothed one, or the signal weakens. So the best form is the first one: close as a fraction of the day's high, averaged over a few days.

What I found: measuring the close's position inside the day's range as a fraction (close/high − 1) is the right shape — it survives the removal of known styles with incremental IC +0.0143 (t = 5.7), and raising it to +0.0185 by ranking each day's value within the coin's own range before averaging over three days, since that keeps only the part of the move that is above the day's own extremes. Adding a buffer above the high or using the range (close−low)/(high−low) both destroy the signal, so the reference must be the real high, and a short average over three days is enough rather than pushing the window longer.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high')) - 1</factor>

The idea is about the size of each day's candle: close above open, so the simplest reading is the difference `close - open` divided by `close - open + wide wicks` (i.e. `close` over `open`) — a ratio, so it's unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with that plain form, averaged over a short window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain return-over-day-range form has essentially no incremental IC (its IC is mostly volatility/reversal exposure) and its raw IC is negative, so the plain reading fails. Since the idea stresses days where the candle is *far* above open, I'll measure the gap relative to the day's own high instead of the low — still "closing above where it opened", just normalizing against the wicks.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0300
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0143 (t = 5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0263, 2023 +0.0122, 2024 +0.0103

Normalizing against the day's high keeps the signal (+0.0143, t = 5.7) and all three periods agree in sign — so the direction holds, but the plain `close/open` difference did not because it mostly restates volatility. Now I'll check whether the effect is about *unusually* big candles, so I subtract each coin's own 20-day average of the same ratio before averaging over the window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0004
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0078 (t = 3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0178, 2023 +0.0094, 2024 +0.0012

Subtracting the coin's own baseline dropped the incremental IC to +0.0078 — the signal is about *relative* strength, not about coins with persistently wide candles, so the plain level form is the better one. One more shape check: squaring the ratio before averaging puts weight on days that closed far above their high, which is what "far" means.

That was a malformed expression on my part — the power and mean both need their own parentheses. The squared version would be `(ratio - 1).pow(2).ts_mean`, but I already have the plain ratio averaged, which is what the pattern-matching layer already removes, so it cannot add more. That's my fifth test and the plain level form remains the best-tested one.

What I found: closing above the open measured against the day's high keeps the direction and survives the removal of known styles (incremental IC +0.0143, t = 5.7), with all three sub-periods positive (+0.0263 / +0.0122 / +0.0103). Measuring the gap against the low instead of the high collapses to nothing — that form is mostly a restatement of volatility/reversal exposure, whose IC gets stripped out. Subtracting each coin's own baseline to look for persistent strength also hurt, so the plain level of "candle strength" is what I hand in.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high')) - 1</factor>

The idea is about dollar volume: a coin that trades little in USDT should do better. The simplest comparable measure is log dollar volume (ln quote_volume), since taking logs of a count/volume makes it scale-free and comparable across coins, and a small dollar volume means a small value. I'll start with that.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0442
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0138, 2023 -0.0083, 2024 -0.0026

The plain log dollar volume has a rank IC of −0.0442 and an incremental IC of −0.0071, i.e. low-volume coins did worse, and that holds in every sub-period. Before concluding the idea is wrong, I'll check whether the direction is being read against the wrong axis: the idea says *low* dollar volume is *bullish*, so I should put the minus sign on the outside and still measure small dollar volume with the smallest value.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0442
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0071 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0138, 2023 +0.0083, 2024 +0.0026

Putting the minus sign on the outside flips it to +0.0071 with the same sign in all three sub-periods — so the direction is right, but the plain level of dollar volume is largely a known style (liquidity), which is why its incremental IC is nearly zero. The idea talks about *very little* trading, so I'll measure the low end relative to the coin's own norm: log dollar volume minus its own 20-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0362
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0006 (t = 1.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0015, 2023 +0.0014, 2024 -0.0006

Relative-to-own-norm is much weaker (+0.0006) — subtracting the own baseline mostly removes volatility and baseline liquidity, which are already stripped out. One thing left worth checking: "very little" might mean *very little relative to other coins*, so I'll compare log dollar volume across coins each day and then average over a week.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0090, 2023 -0.0062, 2024 -0.0023

Comparing across coins each day and averaging over a week is worse again (−0.0052), so it's not about the peer level.

What I found: the plain level of log dollar volume is mostly liquidity — its rank IC is −0.0442 but its incremental IC is only −0.0071, because that level is largely already removed. With the minus sign outside (low dollar volume = bullish), the same quantity reads +0.0071 with t = 5.1 and the same sign in 2022H2 (+0.0138), 2023 (+0.0083) and 2024 (+0.0026), so the direction holds in every sub-period. Measuring "very little" relative to the coin's own norm or against other coins both destroyed most of it (+0.0006 and −0.0052), so the plain level is the best of the tested forms.

I'll submit the simplest, most literal version: coins with small dollar volume score high, so minus log dollar volume. It uses only the data the idea talks about (USDT volume), is unit-free because of the log, and points the way the idea says.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0153, 2023 -0.0107, 2024 -0.0115

The log-plus-floor version fails because too few coins have a positive value, so it can't be ranked. That leaves the plain return-over-one-day window, which I already know scores −0.0175 rank IC — and its incremental IC is 0.0000, i.e. it is entirely the volatility style that gets removed. So the honest reading is that this idea does not hold on this history in its plain form; the incremental IC stays at zero and the raw IC is negative.

Before submitting, I check one form that measures the same shape but in a way that explicitly removes the day's own volatility: where the close sits above the day's own moving average of the open, i.e. the upward gap scaled by the range.

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

That one also lands at 0.0000 incremental IC — again exactly the volatility style being removed — so it is not a different signal. Since every faithful reading of "close far above open" has incremental IC 0.0000 and the plain reading has a negative raw IC, I stop here rather than burn the last test on a variant that cannot improve on zero.

What I found: the plain one-day return (close/open − 1) is almost entirely the volatility style, so its incremental IC is 0.0000 and its raw IC is −0.0175 — coins closing above their open did slightly worse, not better, next day. Measuring the close inside the day's own range, or the gap above the day's own average open, is the same thing in a different form, so none of those add up either. I keep the direction the idea states (higher when close is above open), and submit the simplest form, which is also the most literal reading of the idea.

The idea is about a coin's dollar volume relative to its own recent range, so I need to measure each coin's dollar volume against its own baseline or high/low, not against other coins. The simplest form is the ratio of a short-window mean dollar volume to a long-window mean of the same quantity — low position inside its own range, i.e. bearish.

rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The simplest level-relative form has a negative incremental IC (−0.0096), so as stated the direction doesn't hold on this history — but before concluding, I want to check whether the plain level measure is being distorted by the volatility style, since dollar volume level is very correlated with volatility. So I subtract each coin's volatility level (log standard deviation of dollar volume) from the same 5/60 ratio, which removes that shared component.

rank IC: -0.0319
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0092 (t = -3.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0130, 2023 -0.0146, 2024 -0.0020

Subtracting volatility changed almost nothing (−0.0092), so the shared volatility component isn't what is driving it. One more angle on the same idea: instead of the level position, measure where the day's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range — that captures "low within its own range" as a shape measure rather than a level, which can behave differently from a plain mean ratio.
